claims.text: In multi-component concentrated alloys, strength is governed by configurational fluctuations in atomic-level pressure.
In multi-component concentrated alloys, deformation behavior is governed by configurational fluctuations in atomic-level pressure.
Configurational fluctuations in atomic-level pressure are driven by charge transfer between neighboring elements.
The relevant material class consists of single-phase fcc CCAs made from the 3d transition-metal set V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni.
Changing elemental composition can vary charge transfer between neighboring elements.
The compared alloys have negligible differences in elastic moduli.
The compared alloys have negligible differences in Burgers vectors.
Individual atoms in randomly mixed fcc 3d CCAs experience nonzero atomic-level pressures even though the net atomic-level pressure is zero.
Solid-solution strengthening is produced by interactions involving dislocations and a dislocation elastic field.
Configurational fluctuations in atomic-level pressure cause solid-solution strengthening in single-phase fcc 3d CCAs.
Solid-solution strength is proportional to the ensemble standard deviation of atomic-level pressure, σSS ∝ ΔPsolute.
ΔPsolute is the dominant factor controlling solid-solution strengthening in these fcc 3d CCAs.
The Hall–Petch contribution is typically invariant with temperature.
Solid-solution strength essentially carries the temperature-dependent portion of yield strength in fcc alloys under the stated assumptions.
Lattice distortion and relaxation may alter the relationship between charge transfer, atomic-level pressure, and solid-solution strengthening.
